newsitem.title: GERMANY: German M3 growth to slow, no rate cut seen likely.
newsitem.headline: German M3 growth to slow, no rate cut seen likely.

text.p: German M3 money supply growth is forecast to have slowed in January but not enough to prompt the Bundesbank into agreeing another near-term interest rate cut, German economists said on Tuesday.
A poll of 10 analysts showed they were unanimous in expecting no interest rate changes when the central bank council meets for its regular policy meeting on Thursday.

The economists forecast the annualised rate for growth in January M3, the Bundesbank's main monetary policy indicator, would lie between 4.5 and 8.2 percent compared with the average level in the fourth quarter of 1996.

To allow a better comparison with December's 7.9 percent rate, the Bundesbank also plans to release January data as measured against data for the fourth quarter of 1995. On this basis the economists saw the January rate at between 7.4 and eight percent.
The Bundesbank declined to say when the data would be released, but economists expect the numbers this week as they have often been released around the 20th of the month.

While the numbers will most likely show a slight decline from December's headline growth rate of 7.9 percent, economists said the data would be very difficult to analyse fully as figures early in the year are distorted due to annualisation.

Considering the January data could be statistically skewed and that money supply growth could continue to slow in coming months, Vereinsbank economist Fritz Engelhard suggested the central bank would hold off on any interest rate decisions.
"The Bundesbank might have more reason to lower interest rates once they see lower M3 rates," he said.
Analysts also saw the strong dollar as a barrier to any further German interest rate cut, adding that a further policy move now could appear to sanction a weak mark.

The dollar has stormed about 15 pfennigs higher to about 1.70 marks since the start of the year, in defiance of comments from the Bundesbank which made clear the central bank would be happier with the dollar at around 1.65 marks.

The economists added that the rise in the dollar -- which gives an effective boost to the German economy by making its exports cheaper -- had itself removed some of the pressure on the Bundesbank to lower rates to help stimulate growth.
"Changes in interest rates are no longer needed as exchange rate moves have already acted as a subsitute for additional action by the central bank," said Gertrud Traud, economist at Bank Julius Baer.

Stefan Schneider at Banque Paribas agreed, saying: "The Bundesbank has reached its pain threshold on exchange rates. An interest rate cut could be interpreted by markets as signalling that the Bundesbank is tolerating a weak mark.
"That is something the Bundesbank will certainly want to avoid."

Record unemployment of 4.66 million and the need to rein in government spending to put a lid on public deficits have increased the pressure on the Bundesbank to light a fire under the economy since growth stagnated in late 1996.
Of the 10 analysts polled, two said they still expected the Bundesbank to lower rates again later this year, with eight predicting that rates had already bottomed.
David Brown at Bear Sterns in London said he still expected a further easing.

"We expect a 25 basis point cut in discount and Lombard rate by the middle of the year. Up until now they have done as much as they can, but the Bundesbank has got to be very mindful of problems with the recovery in the economy."
